The rules do not at this stage require anything but a short statement of the purport of the bill, which is to bring the coastal shipping trade of Canada as regards routes, schedules and charges under the supervision of the board of railway commissioners in exactly the same way as that body now has control over the same items in connection with railways. Right Hon. \V. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):	Mr. Speaker, in
previous sessions of this parliament very little

opportunity has been given at any time for discussion of the conditions of unemployment and distress throughout the country. Almost without exception the estimates of the Department of Labour have been held until the very end of the session or until a period immediately preceding a recess, when an endeavour has been made to huriy them through as rapidly as possible. As hon. gentlemen know the best opportunity that can be given the house to discuss questions of unemployment and relief is when the estimates of the Minister of Labour are before the house. I believe the fact that we have never had a chance really to discuss the government's policies with respect to unemployment except at the last moments of a session, as I have said, is responsible for the circumstance that the government's policies have changed as much as they have, and that there has been very little consistency between what was expressed at one session and what was proposed at the next with respect to meeting conditions of unemployment and the situation as regards relief.
I would hope that at this session an early opportunity would be afforded to discuss present conditions. The government has indicated a program of social and industrial reform, but from what has been presented thus far and from what we have been told about the remainder of the program it would appear that it relates not to present conditions but to the future, that it will not come into operation until after the general election and that even then whether or not it is to come into operation will depend upon circumstances as they may then present themselves. We on this side of the house have endeavoured as far as possible to facilitate the introduction and the immediate consideration and discussion of these measures, because we think they are important, and whatever in them commends itself to us will continue to receive our support. But we feel very strongly that any program of social and industrial reform should not be permitted to sidetrack an immediate consideration of present problems in our country.
I might say that there is a further reason -which is but one of many reasons-why there should be an immediate discussion in this parliament of the measures to be taken to meet the existing situation, and it is that throughout Canada the provincial governments are much perplexed as to what the federal government is going to do in the matter. Some of them are hesitating with respect to measures of relief which they should immediately bring in, waiting to hear what

speechtext: I would ask the Minister of Agriculture if the government have any plan under consideration for the rehabilitation of the farmers of the dried-out areas in the west and also for the conservation of water for the ranchers in the same area?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member
gave me notice that he was bringing up this matter, and I have had prepared a short statement which I shall give to the committee.
A great deal of work has been done since 1930 by the federal Department of Agriculture in studying the drought situation in the three prairie provinces. In addition to information obtained from this study, there has also been collected and analyzed, as far as possible, information obtained from similar conditions outside of the dominion. Based on the knowledge gained from the information obtained, the federal Department of Agriculture intends to carry on an extensive program of demonstration and further research, in an endeavour to assist the great body of farmers in this area in not only meeting as far as possible the difficulties caused by the continued drought, but in planning for the future to avoid a recurrence of the conditions in which they found themselves in the last five years, and also to protect themselves if there should be a recurrence of these conditions.
It is generally conceded that this area should be divided into three regions, one suitable for ranching, one suitable almost entirely for the growing of wheat, and the intermediate region lending itself to a mixture of the two.

Supply-Agriculture
It is proposed to select a number of fairly large areas in each of these regions for the purpose of demonstration and research. Because these areas are under the ownership of many individuals, it will be necessary to receive the whole-hearted co-operation of the farmers within the areas selected, this cooperation, by agreement, to extend over a period of years.
The basis of this plan will be our knowledge of the soil and for what it is best suited, the availability of grasses best suited where there is a minimum of moisture, cultural practices for the preventing of soil drifting, and the conservation of moisture, the use of dams for conservation of surface moisture, and the use, where suitable, of blocks of trees as an aid to agriculture. The fundamental aim of this policy is to demonstrate as far as is known in what way farmers or ranchers can plan to provide for their subsistence on the land.
This policy will be administered by the federal Department of Agriculture. In addition, there will be set up an advisory committee, consisting of some of our most successful ranchers and farmers in these areas, together with some business men.

Mr. Chairman, it is customary when the first item of a minister's estimates is called, for any hon. member to take the opportunity to make a general statement regarding it. There is nothing very controversial about this item that has been called, dealing with publications, but I notice that in nearly every item of these estimates for agriculture there is an increase, which would seem to indicate that the government has reached the very bottom of its reductions in the past and persistent starvation of agriculture. Ever since the estimates of 1931, this government	has systematically	reduced the
vote	for agriculture. One would think
that a government that claims to be doing such a stupendous amount for agriculture would manifest it in some other way than by starving the vote for agriculture. To such an extent have the estimates been reduced that many of the services have been largely crippled. I know what I am speaking about, and when we come to the items I have in mind I shall give my reasons for so stating. It is I suppose a matter for commendation to know that the worst is over in this respect. Of course, it is only a coincidence that we find that the worst is over and that a return for the better is just before an election. However, it is better late than never. It seems to me extraordinary that the very foundations of

Su pply-A griculture

our nation, the bulwark of the country, agriculture, should have been so crippled all these years and that there should then be a great legislative splurge made all along the line and also in the estimates for agriculture. Are we going to be asked to forget the dismal past? It will be recalled that in the last century the forties used to be and are still known as the "hungry forties." Well, in this century and under this government's administration this period will be known as the hungry thirties all over Canada, not only in agriculture but in almost everything else. And my hon. friends have contributed towards that hunger and the decimation of agriculture by persistently reducing the estimates for agriculture year after year, until those reductions aggregate the sum of over 84,000,000. I was very much disappointed in the minister in other years when he tried to defend that policy, first, by declaring that the services were not materially impaired and then, getting bolder, telling us that they were not impaired at all. I took the ground last year I think that if any minister could administer the department with 84,000,000 less than it had previously taken-from 811,000,000 to 87,000,000-he should be kept in perpetuity as Minister of Agriculture; for I have never met anyone who could perform that impossible feat. But he was stringing us; he was telling us bedtime stories when he said that the services had not been impaired. All I have to do is to refer to the health of animals branch as an indication of that impairment. I do not know that the government is open to a great deal of congratulation, because these increases would need to aggregate 84,000,000 for the great occupation of agriculture before my hon. friends could deserve an commendation; they would have to do as well as the government that preceded them did in that respect. I recall this, because I remember that when I had the honour of presiding over this department the estimates were at one time very low-about as low as they are now-and it was after a long struggle and an effort in which my right hon. leader and others assisted me very greatly that I finally arrived at the point where the estimates for agriculture received recognition relatively with those of other departments. I do not know whether my successor and his colleagues will be accorded sufficient public confidence to remain in power as long as we were in order to get the department back to where it was. At all events, he has made a start, and there is nothing controversial about this publication vote. I did not quite understand the dissertation my good friend gave with regard to the drought area, but whatever it was I presume 
it was good and will seek another time to discuss it. But how it was associated with publications I did not quite gather. I have nothing further to add at this time. Is there in this item anything that would suggest to me as a member of this house that some of this money is to be taken for the purpose of publishing the findings of this research body or commission? Is it going to indicate what the minister outlined in connection with the various areas? I should like the minister, had it been possible, to have made available the information which he has just given us in order that we might have discussed it more intelligently. He gave figures that are very interesting to me. As he well knows, I represent at least a portion of what might be designated a dried out area, and the mass of figures he gave would be exceedingly interesting once we were in a position to digest it so that we could intelligently discuss it. Like the ex-Minister of Agriculture, I have also looked upon the lowering of the estimates for agriculture year by year with a great deal of apprehension. I have before me now the five years' estimates from 1930-31 to 1935-36 inclusive, and I find that every year the estimates for agriculture have been lowered until this year we do notice a few slight increases, though even at that there are a few decreases for 1935-36. We find three decreases and about eight increases. I had hoped that the minister would show greater increases in some of these items than appear in the estimates for this year, because when you go back over past years and realize the service that was rendered by the various branches of the Department of Agriculture at the then cost, no Minister of Agriculture nor any member of this house can convince those of us who are engaged in the industry that it is possible to give to agriculture the service which is being attempted with such low estimates as we find for this year.
I am sorry that in the confusion in the house we were not able to catch the minister's introductory remarks when he first got on his feet. While I believe that what I did hear is very necessary and should be done, I think

Supply-Agriculture
at the same time that a survey should be made of western Canada. I do not know a great deal about the east, and possibly there may be sections there that need a similar survey. When you consider that there are 300,000 farmers west of the lakes who have been more or less farming promiscuously, I think you will agree that one thing they need as much as anything else is some direction from the department, some lead to show them just what particular branches of agriculture they should take up. I can hear someone saying, " But you have the experimental farms." Yes, we have, and they have rendered great service to the farming communities in the west. But they are not numerous enough and I do not think that the experimental farms perform some functions which in my opinion they should. We should enlarge the functions of the experimental farms, because we have on many of these farms some of the best technical agriculturists probably on the North American continent, and we could utilize the services of these men to a greater extent than we have done in the past. I should like to see short courses established during the winter at each of the farms. I should like to see it made possible for young men living within any reasonable distance of an experimental farm to attend short courses in agriculture, because it is becoming more difficult as time passes to keep the young people on the farms. Unless therefore the government wakes up to the situation it will soon be impossible to retain on the farms even the sons of the farmers themselves. The whole trend of legislation to-day is to drive the man off the farm. We have had that manifested in some of the reforms suggested by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett). In spite of the great unemployment that exists at present in urban centres, it is still very difficult to get men who will be content to go on to the farm and some of the legislation that has been suggested by the Prime Minister in his reform program will I think merely intensify our problem. I hope before we get through with the agriculture estimates we shall have ample opportunity to read the statement of the minister and probably discuss it at some future date.

The agricultural colleges with their associated courses do a great work, but I believe what the boys on the farm need more than perhaps a study of physics, chemistry and a number of the subjects that are given, is a more practical course from which they will benefit more, and as far as possible the boys attending these schools will do the actual work at the experimental farms because only in that way can they benefit most from the course.

There will also be associated on this advisory committee some of the outstanding business men throughout these districts who have carried the load almost equally with the farmers and ranchers during the past four or five years and who are just as vitally interested in the rehabilitation of or in discovering to what extent we can rehabilitate these districts. The survey itself has been pretty well completed.
The hon. member in his few remarks referred also to the Tilley district in the southern part of Alberta. I believe it was in 1922 that that was abandoned. A good deal of it has since come back to pasture. An interesting thing in this connection is that the sandy lands came back first with a native grass called sand grass, but even the lighter soils have come back with a better covering of grass than the original one. The best illustration of what can be done is in a district about seventy-five miles south of Medicine Hat where an experiment was started in 1927 in an area, now occupied by the Gilchrist Brothers of Manyberries district which had been settled, homesteads proved up and then abandoned because the people could not make a livelihood. It had to a certain extent been regrassed by nature, but a development was started there to demonstrate just what could be done in the conservation of surface moisture and in using domestic grasses to regrass this area. For example, a dam was constructed not where there was any stream but just to catch the runoff of water in the spring. In 1927 when prices were much higher than they are now this cost only around S400. Yet with that expenditure there was created a five-acre pond of water irrigating forty-five acres with a volume of thirty acre feet of water. This shows what can be done at very little cost.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS

speechtext:
The house resumed from Friday, February 1, consideration in committee of the following proposed resolution-Mr. Rhodes-Mr. Morand in the chair:
That, it is expedient to amend the Canadian Farm Loan Act to facilitate and increase the extension of credit to farmers, to authorize the Minister of Finance to purchase additional bonds issued by the board and guaranteed by the government, and to amend the provisions relating to the constitution of the board, the purchase of capital stock, the rate of interest, the amount of outstanding bonds, and supplementary advances.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the
resolution was under discussion on the motion that the Speaker leave the chair, certain observations were made to which, under the rules of the house, I was precluded from replying. It may be that I may overlook some references which were made; if so I would be quite content to proceed by question and answer at a later stage, but I think one or two observations call for some consideration at this stage. The hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer), for example, in the course of his remarks said:
We are informed in regard to the unemployment insurance measure the government proposes to carry the cost of administration. If that is to be done in order to help those in the cities who are receiving insurance relief would it be too much to ask the government to carry the cost of administration of this act in order to help out those who earn their livelihood in the country.
May I point out to the hon. member that this question was determined when the original act was passed in 1927. By reference to section 7, subsection (e), the hon. member will find the following:
The interest rate on loans under this act shall be such a rate in excess of the interest rate yielded at the time of issue by the last series of farm loan bonds issued by the board as shall be sufficient in the judgment of the board to provide for the expenses of operation and for the necessary reserves for losses or, if no such bondis have been issued, such a rate as in the judgment of the board will be yielded by the farm loan bonds when issued, increased by provision for expenses and reserves as aforesaid.
So that it would appear the policy pursued by the board is one which was laid down when the original act was passed. So far as the act as at present constituted is concerned, that disposes of the question raised by the hon. member for Battle River. I say at once quite frankly that whether the government or parliament should decide to adopt a policy of loaning money to the farmers at its actual cost, and that provision might be made that the cost of administration be borne as part of governmental expense is a fair subject for debate. I say that is a subject with respect to which further discussion might be had when the actual sections are being considered in committee of the whole, and after hon. gentlemen have had an opportunity to see the bill. However, I do not wish it to be considered that I desire to shorten the discussion. I believe it was the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Veniot) who raised the question as to the cost involved to the farmer in securing a loan under the Farm Loan Act. In the first instance the hon. member complained that the cost of appraisal was too high. That may be so, and it is a fair subject for discussion. I would point out however that the Canadian farm loan board has
Farm Loan Act

charged a uniform rate of $10 for appraisal, and a comparison may be made when I state that the Ontario agricultural development board charges a fee of $12 for the same service, while the United States farm loan board charges $11. It will be seen that even if the amount charged is too high it compares favourably with charges for similar services made by the boards I have mentioned.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext: Would the Minister of Finance permit a question? Are the appraisal charges the same, no matter what the amount of the loan may be? That is, would the same charge be made on a loan of $6,000 as would be made on one for S20,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext: I believe, it is uniform, and I can understand why it w'ould be so. It is not so much a question of the time involved in having the appraiser make the actual appraisal; the major portion of the cost is in transportation of the appraiser. In many instances he has to move long distances, and under such circumstances my hon. friend will readily see that an appraiser going to a farm in a remote section might have greater expenses than one making an appraisal in an area very close to his home.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext: If the loan does not go through, what happens?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext: The provision is that it has to be paid, just the same. The hon. member for Gloucester complained further about the legal costs involved in perfecting security for the loan, in other words in determining the validity of title. In all the provinces except Quebec the board has arranged a flat tariff of fees, based on the size of the loan granted, such tariff covering all services exclusive of disbursements and additional conveyancing required to perfect the chain of title. The hon. member gave an illustration as to cost of perfecting a title in connection with a comparatively small loan. The sum he mentioned was very large and out of all proportion to the amount of the loan involved. I cannot speak for other provinces, but I can speak for the province of Nova Scotia when I say that the size of the loan has no connection with the cost of searching titles. I know, because at one stage I had anticipated following the legal profession and one of my earliest experiences was to spend ten solid working days in the registry office, at the end of which period I was not so sure that I had secured a title to a piece of land which was not worth as much as the cost involved in securing the information I sought.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
Why did you not use the
Torrens system?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext: So you decided to go into the ministry.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext: I suppose the question by the hon. member for Cartier is a fair one. At one stage in the province of Nova Scotia we endeavoured to introduce the Torrens system, and found it a long and painful process However, I do not know that we should pursue that subject any farther, except to point out to the hon member for Gloucester that he cannot jump at conclusions when there are circumstances such as I have indicated.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
Is there a different system
in each province?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
I am speaking only of
those fees which, as I understand it, are the same throughout Canada. There is a schedule, which does not include the province of Quebec of which I shall speak in a moment. In the matter of searching, in view of circumstances such as I have indicated, a basis of fees cannot be set up. It can be limited by a per diem rate, or something of that nature, but the amount must be elastic, depending upon the amount of work involved in searching certain records. The tariff in all provinces under the board is substantially less than the general tariff for similar services recognized in those provinces. To the extent to which the board has been able to control and reduce legal costs, that has been done.
In the province of Quebec the costs of perfecting titles and conveyancing is governed by a tariff of fees fixed and approved by the lieutenant governor in council. This type of legal wcrk in that province is entirely in the hands of the notarial profession, and for that reason the board has no control over the tariffs charged. It has been the endeavour of the board, however, to see that the tariff is adhered to and that no overcharges are made. May I point out that by virtue of provincial legislation passed last year which had for its object the lessening of costs in these cases, the provincial government appointed an official in the person of the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Boulanger) whose duty it is to act in assisting borrowers to prepare their titles. The board has been and is at the moment prepared to cooperate with him having in mind the object of reducing to the lowest possible point the costs to the farmers.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
May I ask the
minister if the provincial machinery will disappear when the new act comes into force?

Farm Loan Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
The provincial board will disappear, yes, and there will be only one board. There will be appointed one chief representative of the board in each province, and if the practice is found desirable we may, under the terms of the bill which will be brought down, have the advice of an advisory board, which will not be a full time or a paid board as was the case previously.
I just wish to say, and I say it in all sincerity, that it was a matter of delight to me to note the tone of the debate which was held upon the motion that the Speaker do leave the chair for the house to go into committee for the purpose of considering this matter. The debate was conducted on a high and non-partisan plane. There were, however, one or two discordant notes which possibly cannot be avoided from time to time, and to one or two of those which slipped into discussion I feel in duty bound to take some slight exception.
One was the statement by an hon. member that this legislation was death-bed legislation. Another hon. member said that at last the government was making an attempt to deal with the forgotten man who, he said, was the farmer.
Well, whether the government has done its full duty by the agricultural interests of this country or not may be a fair subject of debate, but I do submit that those two remarks were not warranted by the facts of the case nor by the record because, as a matter of fact, whether hon. gentlemen agree with the full tenor of the empire agreements or not, I may say that their going into effect had very largely in mind the advantage which would accrue, and I think has accrued, to the agricultural interests of Canada, and that was one of the earlier major measures which were brought down by this administration.
I do submit this, sir, and not by way of inviting controversy, but simply as my humble belief, that no measure at any time brought down in this house has been fraught with so great possibilities for good and of assistance particularly for the farmer as has been the case with the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, and that bill became law, as is well known, last year. In order to assist in the more complete and effective operation of that act there was an amendment passed last year to the Farm Loan Act, which had for its object the making available of a very much larger sum of money by way of loan to the farmer than was the case under the original act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
I have not those figures
before me but I shall be glad to give them, if not in committee on the resolution, when we are in committee of the whole on the bill, and if I may I shall come back to that point in a moment.
This legislation is no new idea. It is with a view to carrying out still further the intent and purpose of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, and bringing this into complete harmony with that act, that we have to-day this further and wider and I hope more acceptable amendment, bearing in mind the general tenor of the discussion the other day, which will materially improve the Farm Loan Act.
I might mention also in this connection the fact of our having passed a Marketing Board Act. I merely mention that as indicating that that measure also was designed largely, if not entirely, for the purpose of assisting the agricultural interests of this country.
So I submit, sir, in those circumstances it is not a fair criticism to say that this measure is a death bed measure, nor that we are attempting at this long last, at this late day in the life of this parliament, to deal with the forgotten man who is said to be the farmer.
I may say to my hon. friend from Bow River (Mr. Garland) that I did not anticipate questions in complete detail which I would expect to have put to me in committee of the whole house, but I shall have the information available when we are in committee on the bill.
There are many reasons which I shall not give now but at a later stage why there were comparatively small loans made under the amending legislation of that year. It was due to a multiplicity of reasons, many of which had reference to ancillary action which had to be taken by the several provinces, some of which deferred their action to as late as the month of December, if my memory serves me right, and some have not yet even taken action. Furthermore, having been projected into the winter that is the season above all others when it is most difficult to make farm loans because the difficulties of inspection which must precede the making of a loan are in some cases insuperable, especially in those areas where we have a very heavy fall of snow.
Farm Loan Act

I have no doubt that there will be other questions, but I thought I should touch briefly on these main points of criticism, and quite proper criticism, and as to which I find no fault whatever, which were made when the motion was under discussion that the Speaker do leave the chair.

speechtext:
I am very glad that my hon. friend has raised that point. He will recall, having been in the house when the original act was passed, that the whole idea of the original Farm Loan Act was to make for long term loans. The short term loan the farmer could more readily secure in the market at that day, but in order to obviate the necessity of his having to refinance himself, at cost to 'himself, at stated periods, it was his desire to have a long term loan, and the tendency certainly was under the legislation of that day that he should get the money for at least one and a half per cent less than he could1 in the open market. That was true even with the high rate of per cent that the farmer 'had to pay, because the prevailing rate throughout the country at that time was something like 8 per cent. But conditions to-day are strikingly different, and I can see that there may be certain instances where the farmer is engaged in a particular type of farming when he would not wish to obligate himself for a long term loan, and it may be to the advantage of the farmer and for the convenience of the farm loan board to make a short term loan. I do not mean short term in the ordinary accepted sense, but a short term of say five years, as contrasted' with a period of twenty-two years.
This question of the hon. member for West Edmonton reminds me of another criticism which was made in the course of the discussion the other day, namely, that there should be some provision to enable the farmer to anticipate his payments. Well, Mr. Chairman, I am afraid that the hon. gentleman who made that inquiry had not made sufficient inquiries outside because 1 can assure him that the farm loan board like most individuals is only too anxious to receive repayment or prepayment or advance payment or anticipated payments of a loan before the period when they look forward anxiously to find out whether they are going to get any money back at all or not. As a matter of fact, in practice the board has always accepted, and been glad to accept payments in advance either in whole or in part.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext: I would suggest to the minister on the question of the attitude Of the provincial board that I am afraid he will find that one of the chief reasons why greater advantage was not taken of the provisions of the amendment of last year was because of the peculiar temperament of some of the provincial boards at least. I have no hesitation in informing the minister that they have been utterly ruthless in their method of dealing with those who have come under the operation of the act. They have been ruthless to a degree which perhaps the minister is not aware of. In my province there have been borrowers under this act who have been compelled, as a result of the attitude of the board, to seek at least temporary relief under the debt adjustment provisions of the provincial act in order to escape the predatory character of the provincial board's attitude. Furthermore, a praotice had grown up there of compelling those who had borrowed under the board to insure against crop failure. While that may be a very good method of protecting the creditor, it has .been mighty tough on the borrower in the last four years. I make particular reference to this fact because in my province all of the other mortgage companies refrain from compelling those who are under them to take out hail insurance if the borrower feels that he cannot afford to pay and is not prepared to do so. But the provincial farm loan board decided to go ahead with their characteristically cruel action. It was therefore a pleasure to me to know that the proposed amendments provided for the abolition of the provincial boards as such, and I can only sincerely hope that when the administrator or the advisory officer under the new provisions is set up in each province, there will be in my province at any rate none of the members of the present advisory board who will even be considered for that position. I have particular reference to Mr. Murray. One might as well know that there is no more unpopular, no more inconsiderate person in that province in matters of this kind.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext: Has Mr. Murray given the hon. member permission to refer to him .this afternoon?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
I come now to the second point. The minister has raised the question of administration costs and I was glad that he suggested that the question was debatable. I think his attitude is one we may be glad of. The question is debatable for many reasons, including those cited the other day when the subject was up. The

Farm Loan Act
farmer to-day in the west, in the aggregate, cannot pay 6 per cent. I doubt whether he can pay anything in the way of interest, in the aggregate. There are conditions which perhaps may make exceptions possible, but 6 per cent is too high still; and if the government really wants to aid agriculture through the expansion of credits, it will undertake to absorb the 2 per cent administration cost and let the farmer have the money at 4 per cent. That will not be all that he will have to pay, because under the three system method of amortization provided for in the long term rural credits legislation, an amount will be extracted each year additional to the 4 per cent to enable the retirement of the loan in whatever time the borrower selects as his method of amortization. It is particularly important that this be done not only in the interests of agriculture, but because the government might very well set an excellent example to all other creditors in the country with respect to this question of interest rates.
I come now to a point which I do not recollect having been raised before. The minister referred to the fact that the amendments that were coming in would provide first of all for the abolition of the 5 per cent cash payment by the provinces on the amount of bonds outstanding in regard to loans made in the province, and that the government would refund that 5 per cent to the governments. Is the government going to refund the 5 per cent to the borrowers or, if it is not going to refund it in cash, will the government take into consideration the advisability of allowing a credit for that amount to go back to the borrower in connection with his loan? I think it is worth considering, and I suggest that the minister take it under advisement.
In regard to the farm creditors arrangement legislation, I am not sure that I share the rather over-eulogistic references made by the minister to the act as it has operated so far. It is true it has been of indirect advantage to the west, which is the only part I can speak of. There is no doubt it has made the creditor a little more amenable to reasonableness; but as to the farmer having been able to take very much advantage of the act itself, I happen to know that he has not done so. And he has not been able to do so for this reason. If a farm debtor goes to his chief creditor, the mortgage company say, and asks them to take into consideration a plan for a compromise of his debt, reduction of the principal or reduction of interest or both, in almost every case the minister will find that the creditor will ask, "What cash
settlement are you prepared to make?" If the farmer is able to make a cash settlement there is no question whatever about his being able to secure favourable terms under the act. But the farmers have not been able to get money even under this act. They have not been able to get it from private lending corporations nor from individuals, for the very reasons which the minister himself and, I believe, the ex-Minister of the Interior indicated in discussing the question the other day. I would therefore strongly recommend a change in this act to provide that wherever a compromise between the farmer and his creditors had been arrived at and agreed to by the board of review, certified to by the board of review, the necessary funds to make that compromise effective should be mandatory upon the farm loan board; in other words, that the farmer should be able to go, with the board of review's decision, and borrow the amount to liquidate his present commitments. If the government will make such a change in the act I can assure them that the act will be a thousand times more effective than it is now, and it will have opened up a real avenue by which the farmer could reach, possibly, a satisfactory position and through which there would be a reduction of debt something in line with his ability to pay at the present time. This proposal I have just made to the minister is in my opinion the most important amendment that could be moved, involving as it does the farm credit arrangement legislation, and I most earnestly urge the minister to take such an amendment into consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
My hon. friend from Bow River will realize, of course, that I am mot in a position to speak offhand and to commit the government in a matter of major policy. I may say to him at once however that his last suggestion does not appeal to me at all favourably. I think it would be a grave mistake for parliament to set up a board for the purpose of administering farm loans and then, by deliberate amendment to the act, parcel out to mine separate bodies throughout the dominion the right to commit Canada to untold hundreds of thousands if not millions of dollars. It will be far better if here and there a case of injustice to an individual farmer may arise rather than that we should not keep control under our own hands of the administration and trusteeship of public money. That is only how I react to the suggestion made by my hon. friend. At the same time it is a suggestion I have never heard from any other quarter at any other time. I do not find fault with it on that account; I
Faim Loan Act

mention that merely as a statement of fact. I will give the matter consideration. I have no hesitation in giving my hon. friend the immediate reaction I have to a suggestion of that character.
My reference to the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act a moment ago was not for the purpose of discussing that act but was merely in rebuttal as to a statement made with respect to things which had not been done designed to benefit the farmer, because it will be borne in mind that we have at the present moment standing for second reading a bill to provide certain amendments to the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act and when that bill is under discussion, its detailed discussion would more properly come at that time. But lest an improper impression go abroad because of the remarks made by the hon. member for Bow River, let me say this: Notwithstanding the fact that he lives in Alberta and is so to speak on the ground, we have absolute record here as to the manner in which that act is functioning, and I may say to my hon. friend that there have been not dozens but hundreds of settlements in has province under that act, yes, more; there have been under the act many settlements which have not been recorded as such, which have been effected by the farmer debtor and the creditors merely because there was this machinery which could be made available.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext: I said that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
For that reason the creditor has been far more amenable in effecting settlements and we are gathering together statistics with respect to a large number of settlements of that character. Let me point this out further: while in many cases there will have to be resort to fresh borrowings and new loans and possibly resort to the farm loan board as a result of settlements arising under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, it by no means follows that that is a major factor in the successful functioning of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, because there have been prior to this date actually on record in the head office here upwards of 1,000 settlements effected under that act which have been the means of reducing the debt of farmers by tens of thousands of dollars and in not one case has there been resort to fresh borrowing from either the farm loan board or other boards, although in instances we have record of the fact that creditors themselves have not only reduced the debt obligation, the interest charges, but voluntarily given to the debtor an advance in either cash or kind to help him on his way. No act will ever do 
all that is expected of it, but with the records before us, and having in mind the limited time in which that act has been in force, I believe it has been amazingly successful, far more, I may say, than the most sanguine expectation of its sponsors. Having said this much, let me say that when the bill to amend that act is under consideration I shall expect to go into the discussion of it in detail and give facts and figures of settlements or of applications now before the board and other data in extenso.
My hon. friend raised a question as to the methods adopted by the provincial boards in their ruthless treatment of farmers who sought loans. I do not know that any good purpose can be served by discussing what is past, but I can assure the hon. member for Bow River that there are very few complaints with respect to this act which do not reach my office and I have heard numerous complaints of the character he has indicated. I make reference to that only for the purpose of saying this: We are now starting a new method which will mean centralized administration, one place where responsibility can be fixed, at Ottawa, and so far as I am concerned-'and I speak for the government in this respect-while we do not wish to throw away public money and there must be reasonable protection of the public purse, if we err at all we shall endeavour to err upon the side of generous treatment to the farmer rather than in a niggardly safeguarding of the public funds. In other words I believe within bounds, even if we lose a substantial portion of these loans, as may inevitably be the case, by and large we shall be far better off by having contented farmers on the land than we shall be if we husband our money and allow the farmers to starve. So, as far as I am concerned-and I speak for the government in this respect-it will be our endeavour to administer this act in a generous spirit, always bearing in mind the public interest, but with the sole object of endeavouring to assist the farmer to remain on the land.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext: The government will still expect the farmer to pay back the loan.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
Assuredly, and there is no good reason why he should not. I do not think any self-respecting farmer wants charity; all he wants is a reasonable opportunity to make good.
The hon. member for Bow River submitted another question and quite a proper one. He said: If you are going to return to the provincial governments five per cent contribution under the old act, because it will be

Farm Loan Act
recalled that in the new bill we have no five per cent contribution, what about the farmer? Well, it has always been a provision in the original act that the farmer shall have credit for that five per cent on his obligation. The only qualifying feature has been as to the time when he will get his five per cent. Heretofore it has been when the transaction has been closed out. There is a disadvantage there to the farmer inasmuch as he has been paying interest on five per cent of money that he did not secure and it may be the part of wisdom so far as the old contracts are concerned to give him immediate credit. That is a fair subject for discussion and we can deal with it when we are in committee on the bill, but in any event I want to make it clear to the committee that the farmer always secured a credit for that five per cent.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
When this measure was before the house on a previous occasion I had something to say on it. The suggestion of the hon. member for Bow River, one to which I have given considerable thought, was that the farm loan board, once a farmer had asked for an adjustment, should if at all possible extend the loan in order to enable the farmer to get a better deal in the adjustment of his debt. I immediately proceeded to secure some information regarding my own province to see just to what extent the farmers on the lands of Saskatchewan had mortgages on their holdings. I find this, which I think will prove to my good friend from Bow River the utter impossibility of the federal farm loan board, with S90,000,000 at its disposal, taking care of the suggestion he made. I am going to deal briefly with the facts concerning my province. The statistics are as follows: Saskatchewan
Number of occupied farms, 136,472.
Farms occupied by owners or part owners, 115.428.	_
Percentage of farms occupied by owners or part owners, 84-6 per cent.
Average size of farm, 407-95 acres.
Total .value of farm lands, $781,124,800.
Amount of mortgage indebtedness, $177,620,800.
That is mortgage indebtedness alone. When the farmer comes for an adjustment that is not all his debt. In many instances you will find that the mortgage on the land of the Saskatchewan farmer is less than fifty per cent of his total indebtedness. So when we come to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Bow River these figures make it quite apparent that it would not be possible for the government with 890,000,000 to accept that responsibility.
The number of farms reported mortgaged in Saskatchewan is 56,587. The percentage of owners and part owners reported mortgaged is 49, and the average mortgage on the average farm of 408 acres is 83,139. So that the province of Saskatchewan is not so badly involved as many people seem to indicate. With the average Saskatchewan farm as 408 acres and the average mortgage as $3,139, the average indebtedness per acre to the mortgage companies is 87.69. With interest at eight per cent the yearly amount due on the average farm on this count would be $250.82. I should like to endorse what has been suggested by the hon. member for Bow River- I suggested it myself the other day-that if the government can see fit to make the interest rate as low as four per cent it would greatly help. The average rate in Saskatchewan to-day is eight per cent, which amounts ;to $250.82 on the average farm mortgage. If the rate were reduced to four per cent the interest would be $125.41, and that saving would just about meet the taxes on the average Saskatchewan farm. Some communities have a higher rate of taxation than others, but I think on the average the taxes could be paid out of the saving of four per cent.
At present interest works out at an average of 61 cents per acre. No Saskatchewan farm land can pay that in these times. This is one reason, although not the whole reason, why we find the farmers of Saskatchewan getting into such deep water; the interest is eating them up. If the minister could see his way to lower the interest to four per cent it would at once cut the mortgage interest from 61 cents to 301 cents per acre. By itself, this interest does not look like an overpowering burden, were it not for the necessity of making payments on the principal. With an average crop the farmer should be able to carry that interest. I think the history of Saskatchewan mortgages proves that to bf true in normal times. But it must be remembered that in some parts of Saskatchewan we have had total crop failure for five and six years, yet even to-day with all those things that we have had to combat the picture is not too bad. At the same time that 61 cents per acre is a substantial part of the cost of production.
The valuation placed on western farms by the census seems unduly small. The average farm of 408 acres was valued at 85,724. I do not think that there is any mortgage company which would advance S3.139 on a valuation of that amount. I do not know how this
Farm Loan Act

federal farm loan board would act in Saskatchewan. As I stated the other day, we have had a provincial farm loan board, and the federal board has not been operative. I was called out for a few minutes this afternoon, and when I came back I gained the impression from the discussion that the provincial farm loan boards will now be absorbed by the federal board. Am I correct in that?

speechtext: The statistics I have placed before the committee, which are given to me as accurate and I suppose can be checked by the statistical bureau, show that if funds are available there can be a great measure of relief given to the farmers of Saskatchewan under the federal farm loan. I shall be quite frank, it has been a great pleasure to me to see this legislation brought in. I am not going to accuse the minister of a death-bed repentance, we are only too glad to see it, and I hope the farmers will not be disappointed when they make application for loans by finding that no funds are available.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
I think there is little criticism arising from foreclosures in the province of Quebec; I have not known of a single case, there may have been some. The difficulty in Quebec is from another source; it is that the board has not made loans, or when it has made loans it has applied a low standard of valuation. It has applied the

standard of the private lender. Due to difficulties largely attributable to the loss of the market, prices of farm lands have sunk to the lowest point we have known in generations. It has been very discouraging to the farmer to find that he could get a loan only of an amount which a lending company would advance. If the farm loan board is going to lend money only on a basis acceptable to a private lender then I fear it is not going to achieve very much to assist those who are in need. That seems to me a most important question, and one which will have to be determined before we can expect any substantial relief from this source. This probably is not an opportune time to discuss details. I recall to the minister that in the province of Quebec the law does not permit a lender to take a chattel mortgage. That may be a good thing; it may prevent the farmer from pledging his movables; it may be protection for him, but the fact remains that a farmer in Quebec is denied a certain amount of credit that is available to farmers in other parts of the country. I have read that it is intended to make loans available at a higher percentage of the value of the land in those provinces where movables can be pledged than in those provinces where they cannot be, and there remains a disadvantage under which the necessitous farmer in Quebec must labour.
There have been some annoying features of administration which I hope the minister will seek to remove. For instance there is the interminable delay. An application is made to the board. The farmer has not the facility for writing many letters; possibly he has not the inclination to write, or the training for it; the correspondence drags on until he is sick and weary of it and wishes he never had the misfortune to attempt to milk the farrow cow. Moreover I think there should be some decentralization with regard to inspection. It may be well to have centralization so that there will be uniformity of policy, but I think it unfortunate that there should be only one office in a province, especially when provinces are large and the borrowing areas are far apart. It happens not infrequently that the need is urgent, and the application should be disposed of within a reasonable time; delay is sometimes worse than a prompt refusal. There is also the question of cost. Frequently farmers are told, "You want only S200, $300 or $400. The cost of having the title to your land examined, of getting a mortgage, of having that mortgage registered and of putting up the necessary deposit to have it radiated, is going to bring your rate of interest, regardless of what

Farm Loan Act
the interest itself may be, up to 15 or 20 per cent." Whether or not it is feasible to devise a method of advancing small sums of money for a few months without going through all the formalities and incurring all the expense of hypothecation, is a matter for the government to decide. In Quebec hypothecation is a rite that is enacted with great ceremony, form and expense. The cost of registration in Quebec is very high. These deeds have to be prepared with the utmost care, and no professional man wishes to prepare a deed until he has examined the title to make sure that it is free not only of anterior mortgages or hypothecations but also of privileges, some of which are not registered. I need not worry the house with this series of privileges registered and unregistered, that exist in Quebec; my hon. friends opposite know that interminable litany probably better than I do, but unless these details are considered by people who are familiar with them and who can assist the government in working out this scheme we will have legislation which, so far as Quebec is concerned, will be like the last act, unworkable and incapable of giving relief to those who need it so much.
In Quebec the interest rate was not quite as high as it was elsewhere, because for a time the provincial government contributed one and a half per cent towards the interest exacted by the federal board. Whether or not it will see fit to continue that practice under the new dispensation is a matter for conjecture into which I shall not go. But delay, expense and the impossibility of getting a small loan-because if you take all the expenses into account the rate of interest becomes prohibitive

are three matters which I think should be carefully considered in framing any amendments to this legislation.

speechtext:
When I saw my hon.
friend from Stanstead rise to his feet I had hoped that we would get his views with regard to some of these contemplated actions of the government. I go back to the question of the Canadian National Railways; I well remember the impression made upon me by the hon. member for Stanstead when he pointed out to the members of this house the serious situation that was confronting the people of Canada by virtue of that degree of socialization, and when I saw my hon. friend rise to-day I hoped that he would draw some such inference from the legislation forecast in the resolution now before the committee.

Further, I can understand where one body should have absolute control over the legislation, but on the other hand I believe inspectors should be segregated in certain districts and that their recommendations, as men knowing the conditions in different parts of the country, should bear a great deal of weight in the circumstances. I am thinking of it this way: I do not believe the minister wants to put on the statute books again legislation that will not be workable. I believe he is sincere in wanting this legislation to do something for the farmer, but in that case it seems to me he will have to go a whole lot further than he seems to be going in this legislation.
I am almost ready to accept the suggestion of the hon. member for Bow River. I believe that where a compromise is forced on a farmer, it is only forced on him where there is no other way. There is now a moratorium in the province of Quebec, and he cannot relieve his credit situation. He has certain assets and a great many liabilities. He goes to the referee appointed under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act and they go into the whole situation in the fullest detail, figuring out what the earning power of the farm is and what the farmer's liabilities are. We will say for the sake of argument that he makes a settlement on a fifty per cent basis. The creditor is going to tell the referee the best side and the debtor the worst side, and when this arrangement is made and the referee makes his report to the court, I believe it ought to be almost compulsory that the farm loan board should advance the money necessary to clean off the debts and put the farmer on his feet. You may say that that is extreme legislation, but you are dealing with an extreme case. This legislation concerns a farmer who has to, or may have to, get off his land for good and all.
As to the neighbouring farmer who has a small mortgage on his farm but whose revenues have dropped because everything he has to sell has gone down to an exceedingly low point, it is just as vital to say to that man, who cannot now pay his taxes and other obligations on account of the high rate of interest, that you will cut his interest rate from seven to five per cent; you would thereby assist the farming communities and help to put the farmers on their feet, if that is the real object of this legislation. This money would not be coming out of the government or out of the taxpayers. It would mean a reduction in interest rates; in some cases for people who could afford to stand it, and in other cases for those who should take a reduction in interest rates. I cannot emphasize too strongly that the working of the Farmer's Creditors Arrangement Act puts the farmer who legitimately wants to borrow one or two thousand dollars and who can easily carry the load in a position where under no consideration can he borrow money from a loan company in a province where the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement legislation is in force.

May I make two suggestions. First of all, why does the government intend to lend such a large amount of money to farmers? Is it not because the farmers have no money? And why have they no money? Is it because they have no farm products? No; it is because they cannot sell their products. And why can they not sell 92582-33$
their products? Is it not because they have no market? Therefore would it not be a good thing for the government to consider a reduction of the tariff so that the farmers might eventually be able to sell their products, instead of being obliged to borrow money from the government? That is my first suggestion and I make it in all earnestness.
The second suggestion is this. The farmers have lost a good deal of money not only in consequence of a decrease in external trade but also because of a decrease in the home consumption of farm products, so much so that the amount which is mentioned for the loan is but a small fraction of the losses sustained by the farmers. These losses are very considerable, and I would refer the committee to Hansard of June 6 of last year. I will not repeat the facts set out there, but the decrease in value of fourteen farm products in the year 1932 compared with 1930 has been $440,000,000. The humblest farmer has lost at least $50 a month as a result of the decrease in trade and the decrease in the sale of farm products. Would it not be possible and desirable for the Prime Minister and the member for Argenteuil, who are two of the richest men in this country, to give of their wealth for the benefit of the farmers who have suffered so much on account of their policy? I make this suggestion in good faith, and if they will accept it they will prove their good faith. Mr. Baldwin did something of this kind in England and he was praised by everyone as a good citizen. I suggest to the Prime Minister and the member for Argenteuil, two of the richest men in the country, that they follow Mr. Baldwin's example.
